item.title: Compiling Matrix Formulas to Quantum Block Encodings
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Synthesizes quantum block-encoding circuits directly from matrix entry formulas, matching or beating 37 of 39 published baselines and improving subnormalization by up to 10,487× in under 5 seconds for dimensions exceeding 2100.

Grade 0.427 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Daksh Shami, Charles Yuan

Figure

Total MARBLE compile time (seconds) on the y-axis broken down by phase across matrix dimension N up to 2100 on the x-axis for three benchmark matrices. Circuit optimization time remains flat, keeping total execution under 5 seconds.

Asks

Can quantum block-encoding circuits be automatically synthesized with poly-logarithmic cost directly from mathematical entry formulas rather than designed by hand?

Before

Hand-crafted circuits or explicit entry enumeration like FABLE (Camps and Van Beeumen 2022), which incurs O(N2) gates and cannot scale past dimension ∼212×212.

But

Counts in Clifford+T+Rz gate set, treating arbitrary Rz gates as incurring O(log⁡(1/ϵ)) T gates. Hand-written rewrite rules capped at an intermediate representation size of 105 nodes.

Tools

equality saturation (e-graphs) · static multiplicity type checking · symbolic matrix forms · OpenQASM circuit synthesis

Abstract

Realizing the promise of quantum applications such as chemistry or fluid dynamics requires building quantum circuits that efficiently encode and manipulate exponentially large matrices. This process forces researchers to grapple with the reality that a matrix expressible as one equation on paper can map to thousands of bit-level quantum logic gates, historically written by hand. Even worse, it often ends with a discovery that the needed resources grow so quickly with matrix size that the quantum algorithm loses its asymptotic speedup. In this work, we present MARBLE, a language that automatically synthesizes an efficient circuit from the publication-style formula for the entries of a matrix. MARBLE algebraically rewrites programs into symbolic combinations of simpler matrices that have known circuit realizations. It analyzes costs of possible representations, notably the subnormalization term that dominates time complexity. It then emits an OpenQASM circuit and certifies whether its cost is poly-logarithmic in problem size, as required by quantum algorithms. When evaluated on quantum applications ranging from fluid dynamics to physical Hamiltonians, MARBLE matches or surpasses 37 of 39 published baselines. On the low end, it automatically matches many theoretically optimal circuits, and on the high end, it improves on a published construction in fluid dynamics by 10,487x in subnormalization. MARBLE produces exponentially smaller circuits than the leading tool FABLE, and it successfully compiles matrices whose dimensions exceed 2^100 within five seconds on a laptop.

item.title: Efficient quantum-circuit simulation of classical control of computational order
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Any transformation with classical control of computational order on N independent quantum channels can be deterministically, exactly, and universally simulated by fixed-order quantum circuits using at most N2 queries, implementable catalytically without consuming the extra N2−N queries.

Grade 0.410 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · Raphaël Mothe, Jessica Bavaresco

Asks

Can quantum processes with classically or quantumly controlled computational order be efficiently simulated by standard quantum circuits with fixed causal order?

But

Universal simulation applies to classical control of order; quantum control of order simulation is restricted to unitary input channels.

Tools

quantum circuit framework · query complexity analysis · catalytic simulation · channel extension

Abstract

We show that quantum circuits with classical control of computational order admit an efficient simulation by fixed-order quantum circuits: any such transformation acting on N independent quantum channels can be deterministically, exactly, and universally simulated using at most N² queries. We generalize these constructions to extended, bipartite quantum channels and quantum instruments, and demonstrate that they can be implemented catalytically, without consuming the additional N²-N queries required for the simulation. In the case of quantum circuits with quantum control of computational order, we prove a similar simulation result, but restricted to unitary input channels (hence non-universal). These results show the limitations of the computational power of these classes of transformations in the studied scenarios.

item.title: Spin-adapted sample-based quantum diagonalization with randomized time evolution
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Spin-completed post-processing of qDRIFT measurement samples eliminates spin contamination, giving subspace roots with spin error |⟨Sˆ2⟩−S(S+1)|<10−11. On an IBM Heron processor, it matches Cartesian post-processing accuracy while reducing diagonalized subspace dimensions by two to three orders of magnitude.

Grade 0.403 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Stefano Barison, Samuele Piccinelli, Alberto Baiardi, Francesco Tacchino, Ivano Tavernelli

Figure

Energy error relative to DMRG (top) and total spin deviation |⟨Sˆ2⟩−S(S+1)| (bottom) versus diagonalized subspace dimension for singlet, triplet, and quintet states of oxo-Mn(Salen). Spin completion maintains exact spin purity and reaches target energy accuracy with subspaces two to three orders of magnitude smaller than Cartesian post-processing.

Asks

How can spin symmetry be incorporated into sample-based quantum diagonalization pipelines based on randomized time evolution?

But

Demonstrated on active spaces up to (32e, 24o). Spin completion requires enumerating all open-shell spin couplings for sampled configurations, which scales exponentially with the count of singly occupied orbitals.

Tools

SqDRIFT · configuration state function (CSF) completion · IBM Heron r3 (ibm_boston) · SBD selected subspace diagonalizer · configuration recovery

Abstract

Quantum algorithms based on the classical post-processing of measurement samples have emerged as effective and robust methods to approximate low-energy wavefunctions of many-body quantum systems on present-day and early-fault-tolerant quantum devices. This paper introduces a generic framework for enforcing spin symmetry within these approaches. We tailor this framework to SqDRIFT, a sample-based quantum diagonalization variant that uses the qDRIFT randomized compilation protocol to generate the quantum samples. We discuss how three key components of SqDRIFT (the initial-state preparation, the construction of the time-evolution circuits, and the classical post-processing) can be adapted to incorporate spin symmetry. We show that spin-pure circuits alone are not sufficient, since the sampled determinants generally span a subspace that is not closed under hatS², and we restore this closure by completing the sampled electronic configurations. In classical simulations of 4-aminobenzonitrile and of an [Fe(NH₃)₄]²⁺ model complex, and in experiments on an IBM quantum processor for the oxo-Mn(Salen) complex, this spin-adapted post-processing yields roots that are exact spin eigenfunctions at every subspace size. On hardware, it does so with diagonalized subspaces two to three orders of magnitude smaller than those of the conventional constructions for the same circuit depth.

item.title: Efficient Iterative Symmetrization algorithm for quantum computing and hadron applications
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Extending a generalized Dicke state of (j−1) particle registers of nqb qubits each by one mode uses 𝒪(jlog22⁡j+jnqb) CNOT and single-qubit gates, using 3j+⌈log2⁡j⌉+𝒪(max⁡(nqb,log2⁡j)) clean ancillae.

Grade 0.396 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Hamiltonian simulation algorithms: product formulas, qubitization, signal proce…” · Nahia J. Dios-Bilbao, Adrián Castaño-García, J. J. Gálvez-Viruet, Felipe J. Llanes-Estrada, Mario Logrosán-Álvarez

Figure

Quantum circuit mapping occupied sub-registers Ai matching mode |α⟩ into flag bits in auxiliary register B using multicontrolled bit flips.

Asks

How can quantum registers be iteratively symmetrized and antisymmetrized particle-by-particle with reduced asymptotic gate complexity in the presence of repeated bosonic modes?

Before

Appendix A of Gálvez-Viruet et al. (2024), scaling worse by nearly two powers of j.

But

Subcompetitive against Jordan-Wigner encoding in the saturation regime where particle number approaches mode count. Analysis covers gate counts rather than circuit depth.

Tools

Uniform Digit Decomposition (UDD) · Shukla-Vedula uniform superposition state preparation · Particle-register first-quantized encoding

Abstract

Efficient algorithms for the (anti)symmetrization of quantum registers are necessary for upcoming few- and many-body physics applications, from atomic to particle-physics scales. We propose a recursive algorithm (anti)symmetrizing the last particle added to memory, each time one is created or destroyed, respect to the rest of already (anti)symmetrized ones. Given a generalized Dicke state (GDS) of (j-1) quantum registers, each assigned to a particle, the algorithm produces another GDS of j registers (of n_qb qubits each) using a mere O(jlog₂² j + j n_qb) CNOT and single-qubit gates, and 3j+lceillog₂jrceil+O(max(n_qb,log₂ j)) clean auxiliary qubits. The (anti)symmetrizing operator constructed for this purpose depends on the quantum numbers of the additional particle being introduced or ``created''. The algorithm improves upon the construction presented in Appendix A of citeGalvez-Viruet:2024hry by almost two powers of j and is on par with the most efficient methods to date, while ideally suited for dynamical memory management with variable particle number. We exemplify its applicability with a small selection of problems from hadron physics which are expected to be addressable with upcoming quantum computers.
